Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=t\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=-\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y={ln}^{2}⁡(t+1)
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t) \\  & =-{sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{ln}^{2}⁡(t+1)(-{sec}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{ln}^{2}⁡(t+1){sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\le 0$ for all $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A=-(-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{ln}^{2}⁡(t+1){sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t)={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{ln}^{2}⁡(t+1){sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.

Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{3}
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{2\pi }{3}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{3})(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\le 0$ for all $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{2\pi }{3}].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A=-(-3{\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t)=3{\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x={e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=t{e}^{t}
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},0]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}t{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}t(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\le 0$ for all $t\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},0].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A=-{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}t(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}t(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x={t}^{4}-2{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{3}-1
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [1,\sqrt{2}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}) \\  & =4{t}^{3}-4t \\  & =4t({t}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}({t}^{3}-1)4t({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t({t}^{3}-1)({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [1,\sqrt{2}].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A=4{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t({t}^{3}-1)({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Find the area $A$ bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t,\,y=t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [\pi ,2\pi ].$ Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $\operatorname{sin}⁡t\le 0$ for all $t\in [\pi ,2\pi ]$ and $t\ge 0.$

To solve the above integral, we use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t & ⇒ & v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }+{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }+{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t| \\  & =|\,-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }+{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\,| \\  & =|\,-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,| \\  & =|\,-(2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi -\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )+(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\,| \\  & =|\,-(2\pi (1)-\pi (-1))\,| \\  & =3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x={t}^{3}-4t,\,y={t}^{2}-1
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,1].$
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-4t) \\  & =3{t}^{2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}-1)(3{t}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{t}^{4}-7{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,1].$

Therefore, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{t}^{4}-7{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t-7{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t+4{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =3\cdot {\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}\,|}_{0}^{1}-7\cdot {\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}\,|}_{0}^{1}+4\cdot t\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3(\frac{1}{5}-0)-7(\frac{1}{3}-0)+4(1-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-\frac{7}{3}+4 \\  & =\frac{34}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area enclosed by the curve (shown above) defined parametrically as

$$
x={t}^{2}-4,\,y={t}^{3}-4t,\,t\in (-2,2).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-4)=2t.
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}({t}^{3}-4t)\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}({t}^{4}-4{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\le 0$ for all $t\in (-2,2).$

Therefore, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}({t}^{4}-4{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\cdot {\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}|}_{-2}^{2}-8\cdot {\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}|}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =2(\frac{32}{5}+\frac{32}{5})-8(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{128}{5}-\frac{128}{3} \\  & =-\frac{256}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required area is $|-\frac{256}{15}|=\frac{256}{15}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding an Integral Expression for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14221452/assets/3dd84b2e84056a4e6c71f7b76534f5a6f1a46132ea5da5ed8edb2a514b9ea6b4.png)

Find an integral expression for the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x = e^{-t^2}, \qquad y = t^3,
$$

and the $x$-axis for $0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{2} \,?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x = x(t), \qquad
y = y(t), \qquad
t_1 \leq t \leq t_2
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
\int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-{t}^{2}}) \\  & =-2t{e}^{-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{t}^{3}(-2t{e}^{-{t}^{2}})\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{t}^{4}{e}^{-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \leq 0$ for all $t \in [0, \sqrt{2}].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A = -\left( -2 \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} t^4 e^{-t^2} \, \textrm{d}t \right) = 2 \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} t^4 e^{-t^2} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14221452/assets/e933e484b931ee54b345a8e7af3b0e44f80a8b019e3e401007ad4987192e33be.png)

Find the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x = t^2 - 1, \qquad y = t^3 - 4t
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t \in [-2,0].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x = x(t), \qquad
y = y(t), \qquad
t_1 \leq t \leq t_2
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
\int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1) \\  & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}({t}^{3}-4t)(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-2}^{0}{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-4)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \leq 0$ for all $t \in [-2,0].$

Therefore, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{0}{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-4)\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-2}^{0}{t}^{2}(4-{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-2}^{0}(4{t}^{2}-{t}^{4})\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{-2}^{0}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t-2{\int }_{-2}^{0}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\cdot \frac{{t}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{-2}^{0}-2\cdot \frac{{t}^{5}}{5}\,{|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =8(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-2)^{3}}{3})-2(\frac{{0}^{5}}{5}-\frac{(-2)^{5}}{5}) \\  & =8(\frac{8}{3})-2(\frac{32}{5}) \\  & =\frac{64}{3}-\frac{64}{5} \\  & =\frac{128}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14221452/assets/d8f08b1cc474cfee367ccf52e2299deaeec146ef7a7a860f64a75f7f7f25cb0b.png)

Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t^3-1, \qquad
y=2t-t^3, \qquad
t \in  (-\infty, \infty).
$$

The shaded area shown in the diagram is the finite region bounded between the curve, the $x$-axis, and the vertical lines formed by $x$-axis and the points on the curve corresponding to $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1,$ as shown. 

We know that the area of the curve is given by

$$
A = \int_{a}^{b} y \:\textrm{d}x.
$$

Since our curve is defined parametrically, we need to change the variable of integration from $x$ to $t$ using the change of variables formula, given by

$$
A = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y(t) \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm d t}\:\textrm d t.
$$

Now, in this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-1)=3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the change of variables formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y(t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-{t}^{3})\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{t}^{3}-3{t}^{5}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t-3{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{5}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot {\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}-3\cdot {\frac{{t}^{6}}{6}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6(\frac{1}{4}-0)-3(\frac{1}{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shaded area shown in the picture has an area of $1$ square unit.

tutorials.name: A General Formula for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve
tutorials.problem:
In general, the area between the $x$-axis and the parametric curve 

$$
x = x(t), \qquad
y = y(t), \qquad
t_1 \leq t \leq t_2
$$

is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
\int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Note the following:

- When applying this formula, we assume that the chosen parametrization traverses the curve only once.

- It's possible that this integral gives a negative value for the area even when the corresponding region lies entirely above the $x$-axis! 

To see why, note that if the curve lies above the $x$-axis, we must have $y(t) > 0.$ However, if the curve is parameterized so that it is traversed from right to left, then $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0,$ and we have

$$
y\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0
$$

and thus, our integral turns out to be negative.

- To ensure that we get an unsigned area, we take the absolute value of the integral.

- In general, care must be taken when asked to compute the area bounded by a parametric curve when $y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}$ changes sign over the domain of integration. However, we won't consider that scenario here.

Let's see another example.
